quests.scene: You missed your friend's recital because you got the start time wrong. She was disappointed.
options: I'm sorry you were upset that I wasn't there. It just wasn't possible.
I would have come, but work was insane and nobody told me the start time, so none of this is really on me.
I'm sorry I missed your recital — I got the time wrong and feel terrible. Can I take you out to celebrate?
I already said sorry in my text this morning. Can we drop it now, please?
quests.hint: A real apology names what you did and offers something concrete.
quests.explanation: Naming the mistake and offering to make up for it takes responsibility. 'I'm sorry you were upset' shifts the focus to her feelings, and the others make excuses or close the topic.
quests.culturalNote: 'I'm sorry you feel that way' is widely heard as a non-apology; owning the action sounds more sincere.

quests.scene: Your team missed a client deadline because of your own scheduling error. The client emailed to ask what happened.
options: We missed the deadline, and I take responsibility. The final version will reach you by Thursday noon.
Unfortunately, several factors contributed to the delivery being pushed back slightly, and we are reviewing our internal processes.
Sorry about the delay. The designer was off sick and the software crashed on us.
We'll do our absolute best to get it to you as soon as we possibly can.
quests.hint: Own it plainly and give a specific new commitment.
quests.explanation: A clear acknowledgment with a firm new time rebuilds trust. Vague passive language, excuses, or 'best efforts' leave the client uncertain.
quests.culturalNote: Clients generally prefer a firm new date over a long explanation of causes.

quests.scene: You broke your roommate's favourite mug while washing up. She's in the next room.
options: I broke your favourite mug — I'm really sorry. I've ordered a replacement, but I know it won't be the same.
Sorry about the mug. It was pretty old anyway, and it already had a crack.
It slipped out of my hand and the handle was loose anyway, so it wasn't really my fault that it broke.
I'll buy you a new mug, so it's no big deal, right? They're only a few pounds.
quests.hint: Tell her before she finds it and pair sorry with a fix.
quests.explanation: Telling her promptly, acknowledging the loss, and offering a replacement shows respect. Minimizing or blaming the mug ignores what it meant to her.
quests.culturalNote: Objects can carry sentimental value; acknowledging that is part of a good apology.

quests.scene: In a review, your manager points out that a wrong figure in your report affected a client decision. The figure was your error.
options: Mistakes happen when deadlines are this tight, and everyone was under pressure.
That mistake was mine — I entered the wrong figure. I've corrected it and I'll double-check next time.
Somebody entered the wrong figure, and I'll look into how that came about.
It could have been anyone's mistake in the team, so let's not start pointing fingers at people or looking for someone to blame.
quests.hint: Say 'I' and say what you did.
quests.explanation: Direct ownership plus a fix shows reliability. Passive voice, generalizing, or deflecting suggests you're avoiding responsibility.
quests.culturalNote: Using 'I' rather than passive constructions reads as more accountable in English.

quests.scene: Your boss notes you've been late three times this month. It's true, and you can fix it.
options: The trains have been awful this month, as I'm sure you know, and half the office has been late because of the strikes.
I have been late, but plenty of people here arrive at ten past.
I'm sorry, I'll try my best to be on time from now on, I promise.
You're right — three times is too many. I'm leaving thirty minutes earlier from tomorrow.
quests.hint: Agree with the facts and state a specific change.
quests.explanation: Acknowledging the pattern and stating a concrete change is credible. Blaming trains, comparing yourself to others, or vague promises sound weaker.
quests.culturalNote: 'I'll try my best' is common but often heard as noncommittal; a specific action is stronger.

quests.scene: Your flatmate walks into a kitchen full of glasses and pizza boxes after your party last night.
options: I left the flat in a state last night — I'll clean up right now and cover the shopping this week.
It was only one party, and I don't see why it's such a big problem when everyone knows students make a mess sometimes.
I'll clean it later, though some of the mess wasn't even mine.
Sorry, I got a bit carried away. It won't happen again, okay?
quests.hint: Acknowledge what you did and act now.
quests.explanation: Owning the mess and starting immediately with an extra gesture repairs trust. Minimizing or partial blame prolong the annoyance.
quests.culturalNote: In shared homes, prompt action often matters more than the words of an apology.

quests.scene: A friend apologizes for forgetting your birthday. It did sting a bit.
options: Thank you for saying that. It did sting, but I appreciate you owning it.
It's fine, it's not a big deal at all, don't even think about it.
Yes, you really hurt me, and I'm not sure I can just forgive you.
Don't worry about it. I forgot yours last year too, so we're even.
quests.hint: Accept the apology without pretending it didn't matter.
quests.explanation: Honestly naming the hurt while accepting the apology keeps the friendship honest. Dismissing, punishing, or bargaining doesn't.
quests.culturalNote: Saying 'it's fine' can hide real feelings; a short honest acknowledgment often helps more.

quests.scene: A colleague apologizes for presenting your idea as his own in a meeting. You want it corrected.
options: Apology accepted, but I don't think I'll ever fully trust you again.
It's okay, these things happen all the time in this office, so please don't worry about it and let's just carry on.
I appreciate the apology. Can we agree that next time you'll name me in the presentation?
Fine. Let's just forget it ever happened and move on with the project.
quests.hint: Accept and ask for a concrete change.
quests.explanation: Accepting while requesting specific credit gives the apology teeth. Punishing, excusing, or dismissing leave the underlying issue unaddressed.
quests.culturalNote: Asking for a specific change after an apology turns words into commitment.

quests.scene: A shop assistant apologizes because your online order arrived with the wrong item.
options: Your apology doesn't mean much if it happens again next time.
It's okay, I'm sure you're busy today and these things happen.
This is the third time this has happened, so I'm never coming back.
Thanks for apologizing. Could you replace it today, or give me a refund?
quests.hint: Accept the apology and steer to a solution.
quests.explanation: Moving from apology to solution is efficient and polite. Threats, excuses, or complaints leave the problem unsolved.
quests.culturalNote: Service staff typically respond best when asked for a specific remedy.

quests.scene: You snapped at a friend while stressed about exams. She was only asking if you'd eaten.
options: Sorry if I sounded harsh. I was just really stressed out and tired, and you know I'm not usually like that with you.
I'm sorry you took what I said the wrong way, it wasn't meant like that.
I'm sorry I snapped at you earlier. You didn't deserve it — I was stressed, but that's no excuse.
Let's forget it. We were both in a bad mood, so it's really not important.
quests.hint: Apologize for what you did, not for how it was received.
quests.explanation: Naming the act and rejecting the excuse shows accountability. 'If I sounded' and 'you took it wrong' shift responsibility.
quests.culturalNote: 'If' and 'you took it wrong' make apologies sound conditional; direct statements sound more sincere.

quests.scene: You had a heated argument with your partner last night and you know you raised your voice unfairly.
options: Sorry about earlier. Anyway, what do you want for dinner tonight? I can cook something if you'd like, or we could order in.
I've been thinking about our argument. I was wrong to raise my voice. Could we talk tonight?
I'm sorry we argued, but to be fair you started it, didn't you?
I'm sorry, if I said something that upset you last night.
quests.hint: Name your part and invite a real conversation.
quests.explanation: Owning your behavior and inviting discussion opens repair. Changing the subject, blaming, or 'if I said something' avoid accountability.
quests.culturalNote: Apologies in text work best when specific and paired with an invitation to talk.

quests.scene: You had a loud party last Saturday. Your neighbor mentions the noise the next day, calmly.
options: Sorry if it was loud, but it was only one night, and it was a birthday.
I'm sorry about the noise last Saturday. I should have warned you. Next time I'll let you know and end by eleven.
We'll try to be quieter next time, but it was someone's birthday, so I think it's understandable that it got a bit loud.
I'm sorry you were disturbed by our music, I didn't think it was that loud.
quests.hint: Own the impact and promise something concrete.
quests.explanation: Naming the issue and committing to specific changes shows respect. Minimizing, justifying, or 'sorry you were disturbed' avoid responsibility.
quests.culturalNote: Neighbor relations depend on small, concrete gestures.

quests.scene: You accidentally emailed a confidential document to the wrong person outside your company.
options: I sent you the wrong document by mistake. Please delete it without reading it. I'm sorry — I've informed my manager.
Please ignore my previous email, it was sent to you by mistake.
Sorry, wrong recipient! Don't share it with anyone, please, thanks a lot.
I accidentally sent you something. You can read it, but please keep it quiet.
quests.hint: Ask for the specific action you need and show you've reported it.
quests.explanation: Explaining what happened, what to do, and that you've reported it is responsible. Casual or unclear requests risk further exposure.
quests.culturalNote: Data mistakes are often best reported quickly; transparency builds trust.

quests.scene: You arrive fifteen minutes late to a client meeting. The client has been waiting in reception.
options: Sorry, the traffic was terrible today, you know how it is, don't you? The roads around the city centre were completely blocked.
Sorry I'm late! Let's get started, I have a lot to show you today.
I apologize for keeping you waiting. Thank you for your patience — shall we begin?
I hope you haven't been waiting for too long, it must have been dull.
quests.hint: Acknowledge the wait and move on efficiently.
quests.explanation: A brief, formal apology plus thanks respects the client's time. Excuses or hurried starts ignore the inconvenience.
quests.culturalNote: In business settings, a short, direct apology is better than a long explanation.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to respond.
quests.scene: You forgot to do your part of a team survey. Your teammates covered for you.
options: Thanks for covering. I was completely overloaded with other tasks this week, and nobody else had time to help me either.
I'm sorry, I'll try to do better in future, everyone, I promise.
It happens, and next time I'm sure someone else will cover for me.
I dropped the ball on the survey — thanks for covering. I'll finish the report section tonight.
quests.hint: Acknowledge, thank them, and take on something concrete.
quests.explanation: Owning the miss and offering to catch up in a specific way repairs trust. Excuses, vague promises, or casual assumptions don't.
quests.culturalNote: Teams value reliability more than perfect words.

quests.scene: You forgot to take your mother to a medical appointment you promised to drive her to.
options: Sorry, Mum, but you really should have reminded me yesterday morning, because you know how busy things are at work right now.
Mum, I'm sorry I forgot to take you to the clinic. I'll call and rebook, and I'll drive you myself.
I'm sorry, I've been so busy lately; you know that as well as I do.
I'll make it up to you sometime, okay? Don't be upset with me.
quests.hint: Take responsibility, then fix the practical problem.
quests.explanation: Owning the lapse and offering a specific fix shows care. Blaming her or making vague promises leaves her worried about her health.
quests.culturalNote: Family relationships often depend on follow-through more than words.

quests.scene: You promised your ten-year-old daughter you'd come to her football match, but you missed it for work.
options: Sorry, work came up and I couldn't get away. You'll understand better when you're older, I'm sure, when you have a job of your own.
I couldn't help it, so please stop being upset about it now.
I promised to come to your match and I didn't. I'm sorry — it mattered to you. Can I watch the replay with you?
I'll buy you ice cream, and we'll just forget about it, okay?
quests.hint: Acknowledge the promise and the feeling directly.
quests.explanation: Naming the broken promise and her feelings teaches her that promises matter. Excuses or bribes treat it as trivial.
quests.culturalNote: Children learn how to handle mistakes from how adults apologize.

quests.scene: Yesterday you stormed out of a conversation after your sister made a comment about your job.
options: I'm sorry if I overreacted, but you knew that comment would upset me, and you said it anyway in front of everyone.
I overreacted yesterday — what you said wasn't meant to hurt. I'm sorry I stormed out.
Sorry I left. You know I get really heated when it comes to this.
Let's just move on from yesterday and act as if it never happened.
quests.hint: Own your reaction without adding a 'but'.
quests.explanation: Acknowledging your reaction and her intent without qualifiers is sincere. 'If' or 'but' undermine the apology.
quests.culturalNote: 'But' after an apology often cancels it out in the listener's mind.

quests.scene: A customer is confused because your website didn't state delivery dates clearly. The confusion is partly your company's fault.
options: You should have read the delivery page more carefully before ordering.
It isn't really our fault; many customers make the same mistake.
I'm sorry you feel confused. Our website is actually quite clear.
I'm sorry for the confusion. Our website wasn't clear about the delivery dates, and I'll pass that on.
quests.hint: Accept your company's share of the problem.
quests.explanation: Admitting the unclear site and promising to pass it on validates the customer and helps others. Blaming or denying escalates the complaint.
quests.culturalNote: Customers appreciate acknowledgment of shared responsibility.

quests.scene: You and another driver scraped cars in a car park. You both think you had space and neither of you is sure who was at fault.
options: I think we both misjudged the space — let's swap details and see what the insurers say.
You hit me, so you should be the one who pays for this damage.
It's all my fault, I'll cover everything, so don't worry about it.
Let's just leave it. The scratch is tiny, we're both in a rush, and getting insurers involved would cost us both more than it's worth.
quests.hint: Take shared responsibility without conceding everything.
quests.explanation: Acknowledging shared uncertainty and proposing a fair process is calm and reasonable. Blaming or over-accepting can cause bigger problems later.
quests.culturalNote: Exchanging details is normal after minor collisions; laws vary by place.

quests.scene: You did much less than your teammates on a group project and you want to address it before the presentation.
options: I contributed less than the rest of you. I'll take the presentation and stay after class to finish it.
I know I did less, but I had exams and a job as well.
Sorry, I'll do more next time, and I'll be much better, I really will, I promise, and I'll start the very next project on time.
Group work isn't fair when some people are just slower at it.
quests.hint: Admit the imbalance and offer a real fix.
quests.explanation: Acknowledging the gap and offering to take on a task is fair. Excuses, vague promises, or generalizations don't help.
quests.culturalNote: Teammates value action more than long apologies.

quests.scene: A service outage happened after a change you released before testing finished. Your manager asks what happened.
options: It wasn't just me; the testing team should have caught it earlier.
I did what I was told, and the schedule was completely unrealistic.
The outage was unavoidable given how the system was built originally.
My change went live before the tests finished. I'm sorry — here's what I'll change so it doesn't happen again.
quests.hint: Take responsibility and show a lesson learned.
quests.explanation: Owning your part and offering a process change builds trust even after a serious mistake. Blaming others or the system suggests you won't learn.
quests.culturalNote: In many workplaces, owning mistakes early is valued more than perfect performance.

quests.scene: You shouted at a waiter after waiting an hour for food. You're now leaving and want to apologize.
options: Sorry if I was a bit sharp, it had just been such a long wait.
I apologize, but the service was really slow tonight, to be fair.
I'm sorry I raised my voice earlier — you were doing your best and I was out of line.
No hard feelings, right? We were all frustrated with the waiting, and I'm sure you hear worse than that from customers every single night.
quests.hint: Apologize for your behavior, not the situation.
quests.explanation: Owning your tone and recognizing his effort is respectful. Conditional apologies or blaming the wait keep the focus on you.
quests.culturalNote: Service workers often bear frustration; a direct apology matters.

quests.scene: You told a mutual friend about your friend's job change, which she had asked you to keep private.
options: I only told one person, and I'm sure she won't say anything more.
I'm sorry you're upset, but I thought it wasn't a secret.
Everyone would have found out eventually anyway, so it's not that serious.
I told Nadia about your move, and I shouldn't have. I'm sorry — it was your news to share. How can I make it right?
quests.hint: Own the breach and ask what would help.
quests.explanation: Naming the betrayal and asking how to repair it respects her boundary. Minimizing or blaming her reaction deepens the hurt.
quests.culturalNote: Confidentiality between friends is a core trust issue.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to respond.
quests.scene: Last week you promised your partner you'd fix a broken shelf. You finally did it.
options: The shelf is fixed, so we can stop talking about it now.
I fixed the shelf, though it wasn't that urgent, was it?
I've been meaning to say sorry about the shelf, for ages. I just haven't found the right moment to bring it up with you.
Last week I promised to fix the shelf. It's done now — and I'm sorry it took so long.
quests.hint: Connect the fix back to the earlier promise.
quests.explanation: Referring to the promise and apologizing for the delay closes the loop. Minimizing or vague statements leave the earlier disappointment unresolved.
quests.culturalNote: Follow-through on small promises builds long-term trust.

quests.scene: You copied a paragraph into an essay without citing it. Your teacher has noticed and asks to speak with you.
options: I didn't realise I needed to cite it, nobody ever explained that.
I copied that paragraph without citing it, and that was wrong. I'd like to rewrite it properly and accept whatever penalty applies.
I'm sorry, it won't happen again, please don't tell my parents about it.
I only copied a small part, and I changed some of the words.
quests.hint: Own the specific act and accept the consequence.
quests.explanation: Admitting what you did and accepting responsibility respects academic rules. Excuses or minimizing suggest you don't take it seriously.
quests.culturalNote: Academic integrity rules are usually strict; honesty tends to be treated more leniently than denial.

quests.scene: A message you sent to your team channel came across as harsh. A colleague seems hurt.
options: Sorry, some people take chat messages the wrong way, that's all.
Sorry, I was in a rush and didn't mean anything by it, really.
My message earlier sounded harsher than I meant. Sorry about that — your work on the report is really good.
I'm sorry you took my message badly, but I didn't intend it that way, so I think the tone problem was in how you read it.
quests.hint: Own the impact and reaffirm the person's value.
quests.explanation: Owning the tone and adding real appreciation repairs the hurt. Blaming the reader or explaining the rush doesn't address the sting.
quests.culturalNote: Text lacks tone, so clarification and warmth matter more than in speech.

quests.scene: As a shop worker, you discover a customer was charged twice for the same item and you need to write to her.
options: Sorry for the inconvenience. Our systems occasionally have errors like this, and there isn't much anyone can do to prevent them entirely.
We've noted your complaint and will investigate the matter further.
I'm sorry we charged you twice. I've refunded the extra payment — you'll see it in three to five days.
The payment should show up in your account soon, I think.
quests.hint: Say sorry, say what you did, and give a timeline.
quests.explanation: A specific apology, action, and timeline resolves the issue. Vague or bureaucratic wording leaves the customer unsure.
quests.culturalNote: Customers usually want the solution more than the explanation.

quests.scene: In a performance review, your manager asks why you missed a project deadline. It was mostly because you underestimated the work.
options: I missed the deadline because two team members were off sick that week.
The deadline was unrealistic, which I said at the time as well.
It was a difficult quarter, and I'm sure others struggled too.
I missed the deadline because I underestimated the work. Going forward I'll build in a buffer and flag risks earlier.
quests.hint: Name the real cause and what you'll change.
quests.explanation: Honest diagnosis plus a concrete adjustment shows maturity. Blaming circumstances or others sounds like avoidance.
quests.culturalNote: Managers often value self-awareness in reviews.

quests.scene: After an earlier argument, your friend asks, 'Are we okay?' You still feel a little hurt but want to repair things.
options: Yeah, totally fine, forget about it, it's not important to me. I'm sure we'll both have forgotten it by next week anyway.
I think so. I still feel a bit hurt, but I'd like to talk it through and move forward.
That depends on whether you're going to apologize first, doesn't it?
I don't know, maybe we need some space for a while to think.
quests.hint: Be honest about your feelings and open to repair.
quests.explanation: Honesty about lingering hurt plus willingness to talk is the healthiest reply. Pretending, conditions, or withdrawal leave things unresolved.
quests.culturalNote: Honest but hopeful language supports repair after conflict.
